'''''Muhlenbergia schreberi''''', commonly known as '''nimblewill''' or '''Schreiber's Muhly'''<ref name=nserve/>, is a [[perennial]] grass species in the family [[Poaceae]] native to the [[Americas]].<ref>{{Cite PLANTS | symbol=musc |taxon=Muhlenbergia schreberi| access-date = 2017-04-02}}</ref><ref name=kew>{{cite POWO|id=409143-1|title=Muhlenbergia schreberi|access-date=11 September 2026}}</ref><ref name=lbjwc>{{cite web |title=Muhlenbergia schreberi |url=https://www.wildflower.org/plants/result.php?id_plant=MUSC |website=Lady Bird Johnson Wildflower Center - The Botanic Garden of Texas |publisher=University of Texas at Austin |access-date=1 September 2026}}</ref>

==Description==
Nimblewill is a grass preferring loamy soil, moist conditions, and partial sun, and is primarily found in disturbed areas. It grows to 9–18 inches tall, with purple to green [[Culm (botany)|culms]] that stand erect when young but bend along the ground upon maturity. Its leaves are hairless, green, flat or furrowed, and are up to 3.5 inches long and 5 mm wide. The leaves stick out horizontally from the plant.<ref name=ncsu>{{cite web |title=Muhlenbergia schreberi (Drop Seed, Nimble Weed, Nimblewill, Wire Grass) |url=https://plants.ces.ncsu.edu/plants/muhlenbergia-schreberi/ |website=North Carolina Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox |publisher=[[North Carolina State University|NC State]] Extension |access-date=4 September 2026}}</ref><ref name=ilwf>{{Cite web|title=Nimblewill (''Muhlenbergia schreberi'')|url=https://www.illinoiswildflowers.info/grasses/plants/nimblewill.htm|access-date=17 September 2020|website=Illinois Wildflowers}}</ref> The root system is [[Fibrous root system|fibrous]], and rootlets are formed at lower parts of the culm. Nimblewill reproduces and forms colonies via seeds and [[stolon]]s, but not [[rhizome]]s.<ref name=ncsu/><ref name=ilwf/> Its [[inflorescence]]s are [[panicle]]s that are greenish, shiny, and spike-like with appressed branches having three or more [[spikelet]]s each. Its spikelets are about 2–8 inches long with each one having 1 to 2 [[glumes]] that are up to 0.2 mm long. The florets are [[pollinate]]d by the wind; after pollination, spikelets separate from the plant and fall to the ground.<ref name=ilwf/><ref name=mnwf>{{Cite web|title=Muhlenbergia schreberi (Nimblewill)|url=https://www.minnesotawildflowers.info/grass-sedge-rush/nimblewill|access-date=1 October 2020 |website=Minnesota Wildflowers|language=en}}</ref>

[[File:Muhlenbergia_schreberi_iNat-92218314.jpg|thumb|left|Nimblewill foliage and growth habit]]

==Ecology==
This species is eaten by the bug ''[[Stenodema vicinum]]'', and is also eaten by cattle and other hoofed herbivores.  The seeds can be distributed by sticking to animal hoofs or shoes.<ref name=lbjwc/> Nimblewill is common around [[Illinois]] where it is native. Nimblewill is sometimes found around [[Minnesota]].<ref name=mnwf/> Some insects are known to eat nimblewill, like ''[[Hysteroneura setariae]],'' ''[[Conocephalus brevipennis]]'' and ''[[Hymenarcys nervosa]]''. Birds that are known to eat this plant are [[tree sparrow]]s, [[song sparrow]]s and [[Turkey (bird)|turkeys.]]<ref name=ilwf/>

==In horticulture==
It is considered a southern turf type [[lawn grass]] and turns brown in the winter. This makes it a lesser grass for northern climate lawns. It is [[Shade-tolerant and intolerant species|shade tolerant]] and tends to spread aggressively once established. Because of its durability in moderately cold temperatures, resistance to some arthropod and nematode pests, and competitiveness with undesired plants, this grass can be used to protect peach crops in the American southeast.<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Meyer|first=John R.|last2=Zehr|first2=Eldon I.|last3=Meagher|first3=Robert L.|last4=Salvo|first4=Stephen K.|date=1992-09-01|title=Survival and growth of peach trees and pest populations in orchard plots managed with experimental ground covers|journal=Agriculture, Ecosystems & Environment|language=en|volume=41|issue=3|pages=353–363|doi=10.1016/0167-8809(92)90121-Q|issn=0167-8809}}</ref>
